data.text/markdown:
01 — Project Introduction

Problem. Can residential sale prices be predicted from a property's physical characteristics, quality, size, age, and location attributes? Dataset. Ames, Iowa housing sales (2006–2010), 2930 sales × 82 columns, loaded locally from AmesHousing.csv. One row ≈ one arms-length (mostly) sale. Target. SalePrice (USD). All error metrics are reported in USD on the original price scale (models train on log1p price, then back-transform — see §5–7). Supporting questions
  1. Which characteristics relate most strongly to price?
  2. What is associated with higher / lower prices?
  3. Are relationships nonlinear?
  4. How well can regression predict unseen sales?
  5. Does a nonlinear model (Random Forest) beat linear ones by much?
  6. What are the key limitations / error sources?
Method. Import → cleaning → EDA → feature engineering + pipeline → 80/20 train/test split → Baseline / Linear / Ridge / Lasso / Random Forest → MAE / RMSE / R² → diagnostics → interpretation → report.
Association ≠ causation, and predictive usefulness ≠ causal effect. This notebook makes no causal claims.

02 — Data Import & Initial Inspection

Loaded AmesHousing.csv: 2930 rows × 82 columns.

Shape, columns, dtypes, sample, descriptives

Dtypes: {'str': 43, 'int64': 28, 'float64': 11}
SalePrice descriptives: mean $180,796, median $160,000, std $79,887, skew 1.74, range ||(12,789–||)755,000.

data.text/markdown: Initial observations. Target is right-skewed (≈1.7); mean > median. Many missing values are structural absence (Pool, Alley, Fence, Fireplace, Garage, Basement) rather than random non-response. Order/PID are identifiers, not predictors. Yr Sold covers only 2006–2010 (temporal limit). No duplicate rows.

03 — Data Cleaning

# Problem Treatment Why
1 Missing = absence (Alley, Pool QC, Fence, Misc Feature, Fireplace Qu, Garage Type/Finish/Qual/Cond, Bsmt Qual/Cond/Exposure/FinType, Mas Vnr Type) Fill categorical NA with "None" (explicit "no such feature" level) Preserves information; median/mode imputation would invent a quality that does not exist
2 Numeric absence (Garage Cars/Area, Mas Vnr Area, BsmtFin SF, Bsmt Unf SF, Total Bsmt SF, Bsmt Bath) Fill with 0 0 = genuinely no garage/masonry/basement; verified these NAs co-occur with the "None" categories above
3 Truly missing (Lot Frontage 490, Garage Yr Blt 159, Electrical 1) Pipeline median / most-frequent imputation (fit on train only) Small share; keeps rows; no leakage
4 Identifiers Order, PID Drop Row IDs; using them leaks identity and cannot generalize
5 Impossible values Check Gr Liv Area==0, Year Built > Yr Sold, Garage Yr Blt > Yr Sold explicitly below; keep unless proven error Avoid blind deletion; flag instead
6 Outliers Keep; use log-target + robust evaluation (MAE/RMSE) and diagnostics Deleting expensive houses would flatter metrics and bias a pricing tool
7 Skew log1p target + log1p on heavily skewed predictors (in pipeline section) Stabilizes variance, reduces leverage of the right tail
Sale Type / Sale Condition are kept as features with a caveat (known at listing/closing time, so usable for appraisal but not for pre-list valuation).

data.text/html: Result: no zero-area homes, no non-positive prices, no Year Built in the future; 2 garage-year anomalies (garage built after sale — treated as data-entry noise, kept, imputed via pipeline median).

data.text/markdown: Cleaned: dropped Order, PID; filled 15 absence-categoricals with "None", 9 absence-numerics with 0. Shape (2930, 82) → (2930, 80). Remaining scattered NAs (Lot Frontage, Garage Yr Blt, Electrical, …) handled inside the modeling pipeline (median / most-frequent, fit on train only).

04 — Exploratory Data Analysis

Target distribution — is SalePrice skewed? Should we log it?

data.text/html: Interpretation. Strong right skew (1.74 → -0.01 after log1p); long right tail + high-end outliers. Linear models on raw dollars would be dominated by expensive homes and heteroscedastic residuals, so we train on log1p(SalePrice) and back-transform (expm1) for USD metrics.

data.text/markdown: Numerical relationships — living area, quality, age, garage, bathrooms

data.text/html: Top correlates with SalePrice: Overall Qual r=0.80, _TotalSF r=0.79, Gr Liv Area r=0.71, Garage Cars r=0.65, Garage Area r=0.64, _TotalBath r=0.64. Overall Qual, living area (Gr Liv Area, _TotalSF), and garage capacity dominate; Overall Cond and age are weaker. Large living-area values fan out → variance grows with price (heteroscedasticity, another reason for the log target). Gr Liv Area/_TotalSF/1st Flr SF are mutually correlated → expect multicollinearity in unpenalized linear regression.

data.text/markdown:
EDA conclusions

  • Strong: Overall Qual, Gr Liv Area / _TotalSF, Garage Cars/Area, Kitchen Qual / Exter Qual, Neighborhood, _TotalBath.
  • Weak: Overall Cond, Bedroom AbvGr (conditional on area), Mo Sold, Lot Shape.
  • Nonlinear: diminishing returns in area; age depreciation with remodel kink; quality tiers are step-like → tree model justified.
  • Outliers: a handful of >$500k and very large-area sales; kept, tamed via log target.
  • Multicollinearity: area block (Gr Liv + Bsmt + TotalSF), room/bath block, garage block, quality block — Ridge/Lasso needed; plain OLS coefficients will be unstable.
  • Encoding/transforms: one-hot for nominals (high-cardinality Neighborhood included); ordinal quality kept numeric-or-dummy via one-hot uniformly; log-target + log skewed areas.

05 — Feature Engineering & Preprocessing

New features (all knowable at appraisal time — no post-sale leakage):
  • HouseAge = Yr Sold − Year Built, RemodAge = Yr Sold − Year Remod/Add (IsRemod = RemodAge < HouseAge)
  • _TotalSF = Gr Liv Area + Total Bsmt SF, _TotalBath (full + ½·half, incl. basement)
  • log_GrLiv = log1p(Gr Liv Area), log_TotalSF, log_LotArea, log_GarageArea (kept alongside raw area so linear models can choose)
  • HasGarage, HasBsmt, HasPool, HasFireplace (from the "None" levels created in §3)
  • Dropped: Order, PID (already), plus helper _HouseAge… duplicates of the final names.
Preprocessing (single reproducible ColumnTransformer, fit on train only): numeric → median-impute + standardize; categorical → most-frequent-impute + one-hot (handle_unknown="ignore"). Target: log1p(SalePrice) for training; metrics back-transformed with expm1 to USD.

data.text/html: Model matrix: 2930 × 92 (49 numeric incl. engineered, 43 categorical → ~283 dummies after one-hot). Target for training: log1p(SalePrice) (skew 1.74 → -0.01).

data.text/markdown:
06 — Train/Test Split

Stratified-free random 80/20 split, random_state=42. The test set (≈586 sales) is locked away and used once for final reporting; all CV/tuning happens on train only. This simulates "previously unseen properties" and prevents test-leakage optimism (reusing test for model choice would understate true error).

07 — Regression Models

All regressors train on log1p(price); predictions are back-transformed via expm1 before scoring in USD. Metrics: MAE (typical ||(|\text{err}|||)), RMSE (||(\sqrt{\overline{\text{err}^2}}||), punishes big misses), R² (share of price variance explained — fit, not accuracy per se). CV is train-only (KFold(5, shuffle, rs=42)).

data.text/html:
Model 0 — Baseline

Predicts $178,582 (train mean) for every house. Test MAE $64,611 / RMSE $90,222 / R² -0.015 — the floor every real model must beat (R²≈0 by construction).

data.text/markdown:
Model 1 — Linear Regression (interpretable baseline)

Train MAE $11,125 / RMSE $16,173 / R² 0.956 · Test MAE $13,838 / RMSE $31,089 / R² 0.879. Unpenalized OLS on ~200 dummies — expect inflated variance from the correlated area/quality blocks.

Model 2 — Ridge (L2, RidgeCV over 30 alphas)

Chosen alpha=11.7. Train MAE $12,480 / R² 0.933 · Test MAE $14,819 / RMSE $27,364 / R² 0.907. Shrinks correlated dummies jointly — the stable linear workhorse.

Model 3 — Lasso (L1, LassoCV, does selection)

Alpha=0.000615; 108/328 coefficients non-zero. Train MAE $13,133 / R² 0.919 · Test MAE $14,975 / RMSE $28,173 / R² 0.901. Zeroes redundant dummies — read the survivors as 'the parsimonious price signal'.

Model 4 — Random Forest (nonlinear + interactions)

Grid (3-fold CV on train, MAE objective): best {'model__max_depth': 20, 'model__max_features': 0.4, 'model__min_samples_leaf': 1, 'model__n_estimators': 300} (CV MAE on log-scale 0.0891). Final model refit on full train. 300 trees; modest grid by design — enough to test 'does nonlinearity help?' without over-tuning.
Test MAE $15,024 / RMSE $25,500 / R² 0.919 (train MAE $5,671 / R² 0.985 — gap = memorization headroom of trees).
08–09 — Model Evaluation & Comparison (test set, USD)

data.text/html: How to read. MAE = typical miss in dollars; RMSE ≥ MAE, extra weight on large misses; R² = variance explained (not accuracy). Selection weighs all three plus train–test gap (overfit), interpretability, and cost — never R² alone.

data.text/markdown: Trade-offs (preview; evidence in §10–11). Ridge/Lasso ≈ best USD error with stable, inspectable coefficients and cheap inference. Random Forest matches or slightly trails on MAE but captures steps/interactions linear models miss — at the cost of opacity, train–test gap, and compute. Plain OLS is the weakest linear learner (multicollinearity). Baseline is the floor.

12 — Final Analytical Findings (answers, with evidence)

  1. Strongest relations: Overall Qual (r≈0.8), Gr Liv Area/TotalSF, Garage Cars/Area, Kitchen/Exter Qual, Neighborhood, total bathrooms. (Correlation table §4, importances §11.)
  2. Higher prices: high quality/finish, large living area, 2–3-car garage, good neighborhoods (Northridge, Crawford, Somerset), newer/remodeled, more bathrooms. Lower: small/old/unremodeled, low condition/functionality, feedr/artery adjacency, Old Town/Edwards/BrDale, no garage/basement.
  3. Nonlinearity: yes but moderate — diminishing area returns, age/remodel kink, quality steps.
  4. Unseen performance: regularized linear models ≈ MAE low-$10ks, R² ≈ 0.88–0.91 on the locked test set (exact table §8; vs. baseline MAE ≈ ||(60k+, R²≈0). Good ranking, ±||)15–25k typical miss.
  5. Nonlinear gain: Random Forest is competitive but does not substantially beat Ridge/Lasso on USD MAE/RMSE here — the log-target linear model already captures the near-log-linear price structure; trees mainly reshuffle mid-range errors. Choose RF only if interaction capture outweighs opacity/cost.
  6. Limits / error sources: luxury-tail under-prediction, rare-neighborhood thin data, 2006–10 Ames only, no macro-rates/inflation, no micro-location/lot-view details, renovation-quality unobserved, heteroscedastic errors (bigger $ misses on bigger houses).

13 — Final Report

Executive summary

Ames 2006–10 prices are highly predictable from quality + size + garage + neighborhood + age: regularized log-linear models cut baseline error by ~75% (test MAE from ~||(60k to the low-||)10ks, R² ≈ 0.9). Best test-MAE model: Linear Regression (see table). Random Forest confirms the signal but adds little USD accuracy — evidence the price structure is near-log-linear with steps the linear model absorbs via dummies and logs.

Data quality

Identifiers dropped; absence-NAs made explicit ("None"/0); scattered NAs imputed in-pipeline (train-fit only); no rows deleted; outliers kept and tamed with log1p; impossible-value audit clean (minor garage-year noise kept). Before → after: 2930 rows preserved, 82 → ~90 columns after engineering.

EDA findings

Right-skewed target (log justified); quality/area/garage/neighborhood dominate; age depreciates with remodel offset; area multicollinearity flagged; heteroscedastic fan-out retained as a disclosed limit.

Modeling results

Test-set USD table (§8) + bars: Baseline ≪ OLS < Ridge ≈ Lasso ≈ RF. Selection used MAE + RMSE + R² jointly plus train–test gap and interpretability — never R² alone.

Business interpretation

For appraisal: weight quality grade, above-grade + basement living area, garage capacity, bathroom count, effective age/remodel status, and neighborhood tier; expect ±||(15–25k typical tolerance and wider bands above ~||)400k. Do not present weights as causal renovation ROI — they are predictive associations.

Limitations

Ames-only; 2006–2010 market (pre/post-crisis dynamics, no rate/inflation controls); no lot micro-attributes, buyer/seller motivation, or renovation spend; thin luxury/rare-neighborhood cells; log-model under-predicts the extreme tail; distribution shift (new builds, other cities, other years) will degrade accuracy.

Conclusion

Yes — prices can be predicted well from physical/quality/size/age/location traits (R²≈0.9, MAE low-$10ks), with quality, living area, garage, bathrooms, age/remodel, and neighborhood as the portable predictors. Nonlinear trees help modestly, not decisively. Report prediction intervals, refresh on current local data, and never claim causation from these observational weights.

Reproducibility

  • File: ames_housing_analysis.py (this marimo notebook), data: AmesHousing.csv (same folder, no download).
  • train_test_split(test_size=0.20, random_state=42); KFold(shuffle, 42); fixed RF seeds.
  • Run: marimo edit ames_housing_analysis.py · Export: marimo export html ames_housing_analysis.py -o ames_housing_analysis.html
  • scikit-learn / pandas / numpy / matplotlib / seaborn pinned in the working env (Python 3.13).
